fixes.explanation: Right, friend. When Saul saw the Philistine army, he was afraid and trembled violently. A king with a whole army gathered behind him, and his body is still doing its own thing. Afraid and shaking, that's the picture the text gives.

The LORD did raise up judges in Israel (Judges 2:16), friend, but that's not who Saul asks for. He says, “Find me a woman who is a medium…” The servants answer with a medium at Endor, and that's where he heads.

Abiathar was a priest (1 Samuel 23:9), friend, but he doesn't show up anywhere in this passage. Before Saul heads out, the text says he disguised himself by putting on different clothes. Then he set out with two of his men.
Yes, friend. “Bring up Samuel…” Saul says. Samuel, a prophet of the LORD (1 Samuel 3:20), had already died and been buried in Ramah (1 Samuel 28:3). He's the one Saul asks for by name.

Eli was a priest in Israel (1 Samuel 1:9), friend, but he isn't who Saul asks for. Saul says, “Bring up Samuel…” Samuel is the prophet of the LORD (1 Samuel 3:20) who had died, and the passage tells us that at the start.

Moses, who was sent to bring Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), is a big name, friend, but he's not the one here. Saul says, “Bring up Samuel…” Samuel is a prophet of the LORD (1 Samuel 3:20), and the passage said he had died.
That's what she says, friend. “An old man is coming up…” she replies. “And he is wearing a robe.” Right after that, the text says Saul knew it was Samuel.
Not this time, friend. The text says that once Saul knew it was Samuel, he bowed facedown in reverence. The woman had already cried out, “You are Saul!” Now the king is on his face.

Yes, friend. Samuel says the LORD has torn the kingdom out of Saul's hand and given it to his neighbor David. Samuel adds that the LORD has done exactly what He spoke through him. David is the name Samuel gives.
Jonathan was Saul's son (1 Samuel 14:49), friend, but he isn't the name Samuel gives. Samuel says the kingdom was given to “…your neighbor David.” David is the answer here.
Achish was the Philistine king of Gath (1 Samuel 27:2), friend, but he's not who Samuel names. Samuel says the LORD gave the kingdom to “…your neighbor David.” It's David.

Right, friend. Samuel says the LORD did this because Saul did not obey Him or carry out His burning anger against Amalek. Fighting the Philistines isn't the reason Samuel gives. The reason he names is about obeying the LORD.
No sword comes out, friend. The text says Saul falls flat on the ground, terrified by Samuel's words. It also says his strength was gone, because he had not eaten anything all that day and night.

Gilboa is where Saul camped with all Israel (1 Samuel 28:4), friend, but she doesn't offer to send word there. What she offers is a morsel of bread, so Saul can eat and have the strength to go on his way. It's a meal, nothing more.
That's right, friend. Saul's servants join the woman in urging him to eat. Saul had first said, “I will not eat.” After they urged him, the text says he heeded their voice.
Yes, friend. The text says that night they got up and left. They came to the woman at night (1 Samuel 28:8), so the whole visit happens in the dark. Full of bread, off they go.
